about: The chapters of two TU Wien lecture notes, Kugi (2015), Automatisierung (WS 2015/16), and Kugi et al. (2015), Modellbildung (SS 2015), each chapter in a family that colours its cards, with the labs it teaches; then each lab's words and practice questions. Chapter numbers, titles (translated) and page ranges are those of the notes' tables of contents and page headers; equation numbers are the notes' own, checked against the PDFs' text on 1 Nov 2026. Practice answers are worked by hand; tests/unit/labs-data.test.js recomputes each with the core and fails if they disagree.

labs.title: Solution behaviour of ẋ = Ax
labs.idea: A linear system without input, ẋ = Ax, rests at x = 0. Start it anywhere and the state x = (x1, x2) traces a path, its trajectory; drawn for many starts, the paths form the phase portrait. The two eigenvalues of A alone decide its shape. Real ones of the same sign give a node: the paths run in, or out, without turning. Real ones of opposite sign give a saddle: in along one direction, out along the other. Complex ones α ± jβ make the paths turn: a focus spirals in when α < 0 and out when α > 0, and a centre (α = 0) circles forever. Negative real parts bring every start home.
labs.law: x(t) = Φ(t) x0 = exp(At) x0

practice.question: Example 3.3 of the notes has A = [[1.4, −1.2], [−1.2, −0.4]]. What is its larger eigenvalue, the one trajectories leave along?
practice.solution: det(λE − A) = λ² − (trace A)λ + det A = λ² − 1.0λ − 2 = (λ − 2)(λ + 1). So λ1 = −1 and λ2 = 2: a saddle, unstable.

labs.title: Nyquist locus
labs.idea: The frequency response G(jω) is a point in the complex plane for each ω; together they draw a curve, the Nyquist locus (Ortskurve).
labs.law: ω ↦ (Re G(Iω), Im G(Iω))

practice.question: The Nyquist locus of G(s) = (10s² + 15s + 10)/(s² + s + 3), the notes' (3.114), crosses the real axis at ω0 > 0. What is ω0?
practice.solution: G(jω) = (10 − 10ω² + j15ω)/(3 − ω² + jω). Multiply by the conjugate of the denominator: the imaginary part of the numerator is 15ω(3 − ω²) − ω(10 − 10ω²) = ω(35 − 5ω²). It vanishes at ω0² = 7, so ω0 = √7 = 2.65 rad/s (Aufgabe 3.26).

labs.title: Bode diagram
labs.idea: On logarithmic axes the parts of a transfer function add: each factor contributes straight asymptotes, and the sum is the whole.
labs.law: |G(Iω)|dB = Σ |Gi(Iω)|dB    arg G(Iω) = Σ arg Gi(Iω)

practice.question: Take the notes' example in normalised form, G(s) = 10(1 − s/10)/(s(1 + 2·½·s/0.1 + s²/0.1²)). What does the asymptotic magnitude read at ω = 1 rad/s?
practice.solution: Gain: 20 log 10 = 20 dB. Integrator: −20 log 1 = 0 dB. Pole pair at 0.1 rad/s: one decade past its corner, −40 dB. Zero at 10 rad/s: not reached, 0 dB. Sum: −20 dB.

practice.question: Same G(s): what does the asymptote read at ω = 0.01 rad/s, below every corner?
practice.solution: Only the gain and the integrator count: 20 log 10 − 20 log 0.01 = 20 + 40 = 60 dB.

labs.title: First-order lag
labs.idea: A first-order lag (P-T1 element) follows a step along an exponential: V says where it ends, T how fast it gets there.

practice.question: For the notes' example G(s) = 10/(1 + s/2), so V = 10 and T = 0.5 s, what is the step response at t = 0.5 s?
practice.solution: h(T) = V(1 − e⁻¹) = 10 · 0.632 = 6.32, 63 % of the final value.

practice.question: Same element: what is the slope of the step response at t = 0?
practice.solution: dh/dt = (V/T) e^(−t/T), which at t = 0 is V/T = 10/0.5 = 20 1/s (Aufgabe 3.33).
